region.en: Kutenai country, southeastern British Columbia (symbolic pin at St. Eugene Mission)
region.zh: 庫特內故地，不列顛哥倫比亞東南（象徵定位於聖尤金傳教站）

texts.period: Told by Michel to A. F. Chamberlain, 1891; published 1918 (Boas, BAE Bulletin 59)

source.work: Franz Boas, Kutenai Tales, Bureau of American Ethnology Bulletin 59 (1918) — No. 26, 'Skunk and Panther'

summary.en: Panther is afraid of Skunk and lies down; Skunk picks him up, puts him into his bucket and carries him on his back, admitting the only thing he fears is whistling. Panther breaks the bucket and runs, tracked over many tracks to a river, where he climbs a tree; Skunk arrives, sees him in the river's reflection, shoots him and breaks wind, loses his fluid, takes it back, breaks wind again — and at last sees Panther in the tree, shoots him, and Skunk killed Panther.
summary.zh: 豹懼臭鼬，臥地不起。臭鼬拾之入桶，負於背上，自言唯懼哨聲。豹乘機破桶而逃，循跡至河，攀樹而上。臭鼬追至，見水中倒影，誤以為豹在河裡，發射臭液，連連放屁，精疲力竭——終於抬頭，見豹在樹上，一擊斃之。

sensitivity.note: Condensed paraphrase of a Kutenai tale recorded by Chamberlain in 1891 and published by Boas in 1918; not verbatim. Published folk-narrative only. Category 'myth'.

passages.text: There was Skunk. He was not afraid of anything. He went along; he saw Panther. He was afraid of Skunk. He thought: 'Skunk is bad; Skunk may kill me.' He lay down. Skunk went along; he saw Panther. He looked at him. He thought: 'Panther is smart; what may have killed him?' Skunk took Panther; he put him into his bucket, carried him on his back, and started. He went along.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kutenai Tales, p. 40 (Boas, 1918); not verbatim.

passages.text: Panther thought: 'What may frighten Skunk?' Skunk said: 'I am afraid of one thing — whistling.' He went along; he put him down. He went along; Skunk squirted out his fluid. He stopped there. Somebody whistled, and Skunk was scared. Skunk started; Panther broke his bucket. Panther started; he thought Skunk was bad. Panther started; Skunk was afraid. Panther went along.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kutenai Tales, p. 40 (Boas, 1918); not verbatim.

passages.text: When he went along, he came back where there were many tracks. Skunk went along; he thought Panther had lied and that he was not dead. He started again; he got back to his bucket. His bucket was broken; he saw no Panther. He knew that he was not dead; he saw his tracks, and started following his tracks. There were many tracks; he did not see where Panther was. He looked for him; his tracks were many. He went quickly. He thought: 'I'll kill Panther.' Panther came to a river and climbed a tree. Skunk arrived; he drank. He saw Panther in the river; he shot him. He broke much wind; he had no more fluid. He took back his fluid; he did it and he broke wind again. He was tired; he lay down. Then he saw Panther in the tree: he shot him. Skunk killed Panther.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kutenai Tales, p. 40 (Boas, 1918); not verbatim.

title.en: The Deluge of Chicken Hawk and Yawo'nik!

region.en: Huckleberry camp of the Kutenai mountains (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 庫特內山地越橘營地（象徵定位）

texts.period: Told by Michel to A. F. Chamberlain, 1891; published 1918 (Boas, BAE Bulletin 59)

source.work: Franz Boas, Kutenai Tales, Bureau of American Ethnology Bulletin 59 (1918) — No. 27, 'The Deluge'

summary.en: At a huckleberry camp, Chicken Hawk's wife is stolen by Yawo'nik!, who drinks all the water in the world when wounded — 'There was no more water' — until Chicken Hawk pulls out his arrow, and out comes the water: there is a flood. All the people go up the mountains, and the water reaches there; they all think they will die. Chicken Hawk takes off his tail, puts it up, and says, 'If there is no more tail, then we shall all be lost': the tail had four stripes, and the water is gauged by them — 'If there is no stripe on my tail, then we shall all die.' The water stops, then goes down, and the people go down.
summary.zh: 越橘營中，雞鷹之妻為 Yawo'nik! 所奪。雞鷹怒而射之；Yawo'nik! 中箭飲水——『水盡矣』——雞鷹拔箭，水自箭孔湧出，洪水滔天。眾人登山避難，水亦隨至，皆以為必死。雞鷹自斷其尾，舉之曰：『尾若失，吾等皆亡。』其尾原有四道斑紋，以之量水——『紋若盡沒，吾等皆斃。』水終止漲，退去，眾人下山。

sensitivity.note: Condensed paraphrase of a Kutenai flood narrative recorded by Chamberlain (Boas, 1918); not verbatim. Flood cluster parallel. Published folk-narrative only. Category 'myth'.

passages.text: There was a camp; there were many who picked huckleberries. Chicken Hawk had a wife. She picked huckleberries. Chicken Hawk went; he saw his wife. He did not know that Yawo'nik! had taken his wife — Yawo'nik! had taken her. He was angry. He shot him; he hit him. Yawo'nik! drank water: there was no more. He took it again; there was no more water. Yawo'nik! drank. Then Chicken Hawk took (pulled out) his arrow; out came the water. There was a flood.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kutenai Tales, p. 41 (Boas, 1918); not verbatim.

passages.text: All the people went up the mountains; the water reached there. All the people thought they would die. Chicken Hawk took off his tail; he put it up. He said: 'If there is no more tail, then we shall all be lost.' The tail had four stripes. Then there was one left. He said: 'If there is no stripe on my tail, then we shall all die.' It reached there. The water stopped; then it went down. The people went down.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kutenai Tales, p. 41 (Boas, 1918); not verbatim.

region.en: Deer-watching grounds of the Kutenai (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 庫特內故地觀鹿之所（象徵定位）

texts.period: Told by Michel to A. F. Chamberlain, 1891; published 1918 (Boas, BAE Bulletin 59)

source.work: Franz Boas, Kutenai Tales, Bureau of American Ethnology Bulletin 59 (1918) — No. 28, 'Chicken Hawk and Toad'

summary.en: Toad goes with Golden Eagle to take Chicken Hawk for a husband because he is skillful and catches deer; watching the deer one morning, Chicken Hawk thinks 'I'll kill her' and kills Toad. Her parents see the body, take it home, and her angry mother says 'Let us go!' — the two lie in wait for Chicken Hawk on his passing trail, take him, carry him back to the tent, and make him perspire over the fire. Blue Hawk knows his younger brother is poor, goes, takes him, and restores him; on the following day he looked for all kinds of animals, and Chicken Hawk and Blue Hawk were no longer poor.
summary.zh: 蟾蜍隨金鵰往嫁雞鷹，因其技高能獵鹿。一日晨間觀鹿，雞鷹忽起殺心，誅蟾蜍。其雙親見屍而歸，母怒曰：『走！』母女埋伏於雞鷹必經之路，擒之，押回帳中，逼其於火上出汗受罰。藍鷹知弟落難，前往救出，使之復原。翌日遍尋群獸，雞鷹與藍鷹自此不再落魄。

sensitivity.note: Condensed paraphrase of a Kutenai tale recorded by Chamberlain (Boas, 1918); not verbatim. Published folk-narrative only. Category 'myth'.

passages.text: There was the Toad. With him was Golden Eagle. Toad said: 'Let us go! Chicken Hawk and Blue Hawk shall be our husbands.' Then he was her husband. He was skillful; he caught Deer. One morning he was watching the Deer. In the morning Toad said: 'I'll go with you.' Then he started; he watched the Deer and everything — mountain sheep, rams. Chicken Hawk and Toad went along. His stone was hard. Chicken Hawk thought: 'I'll kill her.' He killed Toad.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kutenai Tales, pp. 41-42 (Boas, 1918); not verbatim.

passages.text: Chicken Hawk started back to his tent; Toad was seen by her parents. She was taken; they went to their tent. The mother of Toad was angry. The mother of Toad said: 'Let us go!' They started. She said: 'Chicken Hawk passes by here.' The two, Toad and her mother, stayed there; Chicken Hawk was watched for. They saw Chicken Hawk coming along; Toad and her mother were in hiding. Chicken Hawk arrived: he was taken, carried back to the tent. He was poor; he was made to perspire over the fire.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kutenai Tales, p. 42 (Boas, 1918); not verbatim.

passages.text: He was poor; Blue Hawk knew that his younger brother was poor. He went; he took his younger brother; he went to take him. Blue Hawk restored his younger brother. On the following day he looked for all kinds of animals. He was well. Chicken Hawk and Blue Hawk were no longer poor.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kutenai Tales, p. 42 (Boas, 1918); not verbatim.

region.en: Race-course of the Kutenai plains (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 庫特內平原賽道（象徵定位）

texts.period: Told by Michel to A. F. Chamberlain, 1891; published 1918 (Boas, BAE Bulletin 59)

source.work: Franz Boas, Kutenai Tales, Bureau of American Ethnology Bulletin 59 (1918) — No. 29, 'Race of Frog and Antelope'

summary.en: Frog proposes to race Antelope, a fast runner never beaten; going to his tent, Frog tells all the Frogs 'Do this' — and all the Frogs lie down along the course. Frog puts down her clothes, Antelope puts down his, and they start; Antelope does not run fast, and Frog goes fast, gets ahead of Antelope, takes her clothes, and starts again — while all the Frogs lie there. Antelope was hungry and thirsty; in the evening all the Frogs started and got ahead of Antelope.
summary.zh: 蛙倡言與羚羊賽跑——羚羊善跑，從未落敗。至其帳，蛙呼眾蛙『照做』，群蛙沿道而臥。蛙與羚羊各自寬衣；起跑之後，羚羊未全力，蛙卻飛奔而前，先行脫衣換位——群蛙則沿途輪番臥伏。羚羊飢渴難耐；入夜，群蛙競發，又超羚羊而去。

sensitivity.note: Condensed paraphrase of a Kutenai tale recorded by Chamberlain (Boas, 1918); not verbatim. Relay-race trickster episode. Published folk-narrative only. Category 'myth'.

passages.text: There was Frog. He said: 'Let us go to Antelope's tent! We will race with him.' Antelope was a fast runner; he was never beaten in racing. Frog arrived there. He said to all the Frogs: 'Do this.' All the Frogs lay down. (Frog) put down all her clothes; Antelope put down his clothes. Then he ran fast: they two stood together. He started.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kutenai Tales, p. 42 (Boas, 1918); not verbatim.

passages.text: Antelope did not run fast. Then Frog went fast, got ahead of Antelope, and took her clothes; she started again. All the Frogs were lying there. (Antelope) was hungry and thirsty. In the evening all the Frogs started; they got ahead of Antelope.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kutenai Tales, p. 42 (Boas, 1918); not verbatim.

region.en: Giant's killing-ground on the Kutenai trail (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 庫特內小道上巨人殺戮之地（象徵定位）

texts.period: Told by Michel to A. F. Chamberlain, 1891; published 1918 (Boas, BAE Bulletin 59)

source.work: Franz Boas, Kutenai Tales, Bureau of American Ethnology Bulletin 59 (1918) — No. 30, 'The Woman and the Giant'

summary.en: The Indians travelling along are killed by a Giant, and none return to their tents; one woman with a child starts and meets him. Asked 'What is it?', she says, 'This is your younger brother' — and to 'What did you do to make him so white?' she answers, 'I cooked him to make him white.' The Giant says, 'Cook me likewise,' and she does: when she puts her forked stick into the fire the Giant says, 'Tseika'tkeil' ('It is hot!') — and the woman thrusts him in and he dies.
summary.zh: 印第安人行旅為巨人所殺，無一生還。一婦携子出行，遇巨人。巨人問：『此為何物？』婦答：『此乃你弟弟。』又問：『何以使它如此白嫩？』答：『煮過才白。』巨人曰：『也把我煮了吧！』婦人燒火，將分叉木杖插入火中；巨人呼『燙！』——婦人將他推入火中，巨人遂死。

sensitivity.note: Condensed paraphrase of a Kutenai tale recorded by Chamberlain (Boas, 1918); not verbatim. Published folk-narrative only. Category 'myth'.

passages.text: There were the Indians. They started; they went along. They saw a Giant, who killed them; they did not return to their tents. One woman started; she had a child. She went along; she saw the Giant. She said to him: 'What is it?' The Giant said: 'What are you doing?' The woman said to him: 'This is your younger brother.' He said: 'What did you do to make him so white?' She said to him: 'I cooked him to make him white.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kutenai Tales, pp. 42-43 (Boas, 1918); not verbatim.

passages.text: He said: 'Cook me likewise.' She cooked him likewise. Then he said: 'Push it in (with the forked stick).' She put her forked stick into the fire. The Giant said: 'Tseika'tkeil' — it is hot. Then the woman thrust him in, and he died. Enough.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kutenai Tales, p. 43 (Boas, 1918); not verbatim.

title.en: The Sun: Chicken Hawk Proves the Better Sun

region.en: Sun-making place far away (symbolic pin in Kutenai country)
region.zh: 遠方製日之所（象徵定位於庫特內故地）

texts.period: Told by Angi McLaughlin (Lower Kutenai); collected by A. F. Chamberlain, 1891; published 1918 (Boas, BAE Bulletin 59)

source.work: Franz Boas, Kutenai Tales, Bureau of American Ethnology Bulletin 59 (1918) — No. 33, 'The Sun'

summary.en: Coyote travels with Chicken Hawk to the far place where the people are making the sun; Coyote claims 'I'll be the sun' first, Chicken Hawk claims 'I first', and Coyote refuses. On the way Chicken Hawk teaches the test: grease will be there, and when people pass they bite off a piece. Chicken Hawk bites off his piece and passes; Coyote takes it, the grease falls down, and Coyote goes rolling along. In the evening Coyote says 'I first', and sets out early — after a little while it is evening: Coyote is a bad sun. 'Now I, now I myself shall start,' says Chicken Hawk, and the sun rises: Chicken Hawk was a good sun. Coyote, angry, thinks to shoot Chicken Hawk — his arrow and his bow are all burned, the earth all burned; running with everything on fire, he comes to a trail and lies down there: the trail did not burn. 'I am glad that I am not dead.'
summary.zh: 郊狼與雞鷹同赴遠方製日之地。郊狼搶言『吾先為日』，雞鷹亦稱『我先』，郊狼不允。途中雞鷹授以試煉之法：彼處有油脂，行人經過皆咬取一片。雞鷹咬而過；郊狼咬之，油脂墜地，滾落塵埃。傍晚郊狼搶先昇日，未幾天又黑——郊狼乃劣日。雞鷹曰：『如今輪到我了！』遂昇日——雞鷹乃善日。郊狼怒欲射之；其箭其弓俱化為灰，大地盡焚。他奔逃於火海之中，得一道路，臥其上——道路未焚。郊狼曰：『幸而不死。』

sensitivity.note: Condensed paraphrase of a Kutenai sun-making narrative recorded by Chamberlain (Boas, 1918); not verbatim. Published folk-narrative only. Category 'myth'.

passages.text: Coyote went along with Chicken Hawk. Coyote said: 'Let us go there far away, where the people are making the sun.' Coyote said first: 'I'll be the sun.' (Chicken Hawk said:) 'I first.' Coyote said: 'No.' Then they started; they went along. Chicken Hawk said: 'You shall listen to me.' Coyote said: 'What is it?' Chicken Hawk said: 'It is where we are going.' Coyote said: 'What is it?' (Chicken Hawk said:) 'Then we'll stay over there. There will be grease. When people pass, they bite off a piece.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kutenai Tales, p. 48 (Boas, 1918); not verbatim.

passages.text: They arrived there; Chicken Hawk bit off a piece. 'Now you,' said Chicken Hawk. Then Chicken Hawk passed; then Coyote took it. The grease fell down; Coyote went rolling along. Then Coyote started; he went quickly. Chicken Hawk overtook him: 'Listen to me, what I tell you' — then he did not speak. They arrived there; then in the evening Coyote said: 'I first.' Chicken Hawk said: 'No.' Then they started early. After a little while it was evening; Coyote arrived. The people said: 'Coyote is bad.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kutenai Tales, p. 48 (Boas, 1918); not verbatim.

passages.text: After a little while Chicken Hawk said: 'Now I, now I myself shall start.' Thus spoke Chicken Hawk; then the sun rose. Chicken Hawk was a good sun. Coyote was angry; he thought he would shoot Chicken Hawk. Coyote's arrow burned; his arrow and his bow were all burned; he put it down. The earth was all burned. He started running, and everything was on fire; he did not know what to do. He came to a trail and lay down there; the trail did not burn. Then Coyote said: 'I am glad that I am not dead.' Enough.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kutenai Tales, p. 48 (Boas, 1918); not verbatim.

title.en: Fox and Skunk: The Pot and the Whistle

region.en: River-drinking place of the Kutenai trail (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 庫特內小道河畔飲水處（象徵定位）

texts.period: Told by Angi McLaughlin (Lower Kutenai); collected by A. F. Chamberlain, 1891; published 1918 (Boas, BAE Bulletin 59)

source.work: Franz Boas, Kutenai Tales, Bureau of American Ethnology Bulletin 59 (1918) — No. 34, 'Fox and Skunk'

summary.en: Skunk goes along carrying Fox in his pot, saying 'There is nothing I am afraid of — the only thing I am afraid of is whistling'; the sound of whistling comes, Skunk runs away, and Fox breaks the pot and starts. Skunk arrives and sees his pot broken, cries, and thinks he will kill Fox. Coming to a river to drink, he sees Fox inside the water, squirts his fluid at him, becomes tired, lies down and looks up — Fox is above; he turns around to squirt again, but Fox shot him. Enough.
summary.zh: 臭鼬負鍋而行，鍋中藏狐。臭鼬自誇無所畏懼——『唯懼哨聲』。哨聲忽起，臭鼬大驚而逃；狐趁機破鍋而去。臭鼬至，見鍋破，哭而思復仇。至河欲飲，見水中狐影，噴射臭液；力竭臥地仰視——狐竟在其上方。他翻身欲再噴，狐一箭將其射死。

sensitivity.note: Condensed paraphrase of a Kutenai tale recorded by Chamberlain (Boas, 1918); not verbatim. Published folk-narrative only. Category 'myth'.

passages.text: Skunk was going along. There was Fox; he carried a pot (that is, Fox was in the pot that Skunk was carrying). He wanted to sit down; he put down his pot. He went along. (Skunk) said: 'There is nothing I am afraid of.' He said: 'The only thing I am afraid of is whistling.' Then he sat down; Fox arose. There was the sound of whistling; Skunk ran away. Fox broke the pot; Fox started.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kutenai Tales, p. 48 (Boas, 1918); not verbatim.

passages.text: Skunk arrived; he saw that his pot was broken. He cried; he thought he would kill Fox. Then Skunk started. He saw a river; he was going to drink. He saw Fox inside the water; then he squirted his fluid at him. He became tired; he lay down and looked up. He saw Fox, being above. Then he turned around; he thought he would squirt his fluid at him, but Fox shot him. Enough.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kutenai Tales, pp. 48-49 (Boas, 1918); not verbatim.

region.en: Young-grass meadows of the Kutenai (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 庫特內嫩草草甸（象徵定位）

texts.period: Told by Angi McLaughlin (Lower Kutenai); collected by A. F. Chamberlain, 1891; published 1918 (Boas, BAE Bulletin 59)

source.work: Franz Boas, Kutenai Tales, Bureau of American Ethnology Bulletin 59 (1918) — No. 35, 'Coyote and Caribou'

summary.en: There were two — Coyote and Caribou. Caribou started; Coyote was angry and thought he would kill Caribou, asking, 'Why does it take you so long?' Caribou said, 'I eat small grass and I quickly get fat.' Coyote killed Caribou; Coyote came along, entered Caribou's tent — Caribou was dead. Coyote cried and said, 'I loved my friend.' Enough.
summary.zh: 郊狼與馴鹿同行。馴鹿先行；郊狼怒而欲殺之，問：『為何如此遲緩？』馴鹿答：『我食嫩草，易於長肥。』郊狼遂誅馴鹿，入其帳——鹿已死。郊狼哭曰：『吾深愛吾友。』

sensitivity.note: Condensed paraphrase of a Kutenai tale recorded by Chamberlain (Boas, 1918); not verbatim. Published folk-narrative only. Category 'myth'.

passages.text: There were two — (Coyote and) Caribou. Caribou started; Coyote was angry. He thought he would kill Caribou. Coyote said: 'Why does it take you so long?' Caribou said: 'I eat small grass and I quickly get fat.' Coyote killed Caribou; Coyote came along. He entered (Caribou's) tent; Caribou was dead. Coyote cried. He said: 'I loved my friend.' Enough.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kutenai Tales, p. 51 (Boas, 1918); not verbatim.

title.en: Coyote and Owl: The Child-Stealer Danced to Death

region.en: Evening camp where Owl steals children (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 鴞夜竊孩童之營地（象徵定位）

texts.period: Told by Angi McLaughlin (Lower Kutenai); collected by A. F. Chamberlain, 1891; published 1918 (Boas, BAE Bulletin 59)

source.work: Franz Boas, Kutenai Tales, Bureau of American Ethnology Bulletin 59 (1918) — No. 36, 'Coyote and Owl'

summary.en: Owl stole children; Coyote said, 'I'll be a child,' and cried in the evening — 'You make a bad noise; Owl may almost take you away,' he was told, and Coyote was taken. He was thrown out of the doorway and Owl took him along; carrying him along, Coyote said, 'I am Coyote.' Owl was told, 'Let us dance!' — Coyote and Owl danced, and Coyote killed Owl, who had stolen the children. They started back, and he said, 'I killed Owl.' Enough.
summary.zh: 鴞專竊孩童。郊狼自言『吾扮孩童』，夜間啼哭——人告之：『哭聲太兇，鴞幾乎要來抓你了。』郊狼果被擄，拋出門外，為鴞所負。途中郊狼自報：『我是郊狼。』有人對鴞說：『我們跳舞吧！』郊狼與鴞共舞，郊狼趁機誅殺這個偷孩子的鴞。他返回後宣告：『我殺了鴞。』

sensitivity.note: Condensed paraphrase of a Kutenai tale recorded by Chamberlain (Boas, 1918); not verbatim. Published folk-narrative only. Category 'myth'.

passages.text: Owl stole children. Coyote said: 'I'll be a child.' Coyote cried in the evening. He was told: 'You make a bad noise; Owl may almost take you away.' Coyote was taken; he was thrown out of the doorway. Owl took him along; he carried him along. He said: 'I am Coyote.' Owl was told: 'Let us dance!' Coyote and Owl danced; Coyote killed Owl, who had stolen the children. They started back. He said: 'I killed Owl.' Enough.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kutenai Tales, p. 51 (Boas, 1918); not verbatim.

title.en: Coyote and Deer: The Talking War-Bonnet
title.zh: 郊狼與鹿：會說話的戰盔

region.en: Windy trail where the head is held in the hand (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 風中小道，手托人頭之處（象徵定位）

texts.period: Told by Angi McLaughlin (Lower Kutenai); collected by A. F. Chamberlain, 1891; published 1918 (Boas, BAE Bulletin 59)

source.work: Franz Boas, Kutenai Tales, Bureau of American Ethnology Bulletin 59 (1918) — No. 37, 'Coyote and Deer'

summary.en: Coyote went along and saw Deer, and thought he would kill him; the wind was blowing and frightened him. He did thus to it, and went on; he stood there holding his head in the hand. Coyote said, 'Is that your father's war bonnet?' — and the thing said, 'What is it? Do you forget that you killed me?' Coyote said, 'I thought it was nothing.' Enough.
summary.zh: 郊狼行路遇鹿，欲殺之；風起，將其嚇退。他如此對付風，繼續前行；途中見一手托之人頭。郊狼問：『這是你父親的戰盔嗎？』人頭答：『什麼？你忘了是你殺了我嗎？』郊狼曰：『我以為無妨。』

sensitivity.note: Condensed paraphrase of a Kutenai tale recorded by Chamberlain (Boas, 1918); not verbatim. Published folk-narrative only. Category 'myth'.

passages.text: He went along; he saw Deer. He thought he would kill him; the wind was blowing and frightened him. He did thus to it; he went on. He stood there holding (in the hand) his head thus. Coyote said: 'Is that your father's war bonnet?' The thing said: 'What is it? Do you forget that you killed me?' Coyote said: 'I thought it was nothing.' Enough.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kutenai Tales, p. 51 (Boas, 1918); not verbatim.
